newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Switzerland to keep easy money policy in '97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Switzerland to keep easy money policy in '97.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) said on Friday it would extend its generous monetary policy into 1997 and not push up interest rates until there were clear signs that Switzerland's stagnant economy was growing again.
But it warned financial markets not to expect any more official rate cuts soon, stressing it had already done its part to stimulate growth that has stayed basically flat since 1990.

"The board of the Swiss National Bank, in agreement with the Swiss government, is continuing its easier monetary policy," the SNB said in a statement at its year-end news conference, citing the weak economy and uncertainty about Europe's single currency.

Its benchmark seasonally adjusted central bank money supply would exceed the medium-term target of one percent annual growth again next year, it added. It put the 1996 rise at around 4.5 percent in the fourth quarter compared with the year-ago period.

"The supply of money will remain abundant, creating the monetary preconditions for economic recovery," it pledged, although it reserved the right to change course should conditions on financial markets warrant this.
The SNB said its three-man policy-making board considered the current inflation risk in Switzerland to be slight, putting its projection for average 1997 inflation at one percent.
"Nevertheless, it is aware that the time for a change of direction must be carefully chosen if price stability is to be maintained in the medium term," the SNB said.
"A change in monetary policy, however, will only enter into consideration once the Swiss economy is clearly on an uptrend."
SNB Chairman Hans Meyer said picking the time to start tightening policy again before inflationary pressure drove prices higher remained the central bank's biggest challenge.
"Timing is of the essence," he told reporters.
The SNB started easing policy in mid-1995 and has generously pumped liqudity into the banking system since late July to weaken an overvalued Swiss franc and boost the economy by spurring exports.
It cemented the move by cutting the discount rate by 50 basis points in September to match a record low 1.0 percent.
Asked whether more cuts were possible if the economy keeps heading lower, Meyer said the SNB felt it had done its part.
"This implies the view that we don't think monetary policy would play the central role in the immediate future. However in the end, never say never," Meyer said.
The SNB said it expected Swiss real gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by around 0.5 percent next year, revising down its previous forecast of 1.0 to 1.5 percent growth.
Meyer said the bank would watch a broad range of indicators to decide when the time was ripe to start tightening policy.
Officials expressed satisfaction that the Swiss franc had come off highs against the dollar and mark touched this year on investor fears that the new euro currency would be unstable.
Many investors saw the solid franc as a safe haven currency, but have since been deterred by low Swiss interest rates.
"I would certainly no longer say the franc is clearly overvalued," SNB board member Bruno Gehrig said. Asked whether it was properly valued, Gehrig said: "It's justifiably valued."
Short-term money rates were marginally lower and the franc slightly firmer after the SNB comments. Markets had expected the SNB to keep policy loose.
Analysts seized on the SNB statement it planned to overshoot the one percent target for money supply growth in 1997.

"The SNB will have to lower interest rates quite substantially to achieve or even surpass the one percent target," CS Research said, saying base money would be expected to shrink as Swiss increasingly favour credit cards over cash.
